title: Bury yourself
hookLine: bury your existence in the earth of obscurity, for what grows unburied doesn't flower (Hikam 11, paraphrased)
tomorrow: you asked and asked, and the answer is 'not yet.' now what?

lines: A KID IN BLACK MOVES THE STAIRS.
cards: Opening night of the school musical. Between scenes the lights drop to black, and a kid dressed all in black slips onstage, drags a staircase into place, and is gone before the lights come back up.
Nobody claps for the staircase. At the bows, the leads get flowers. The crew is still in the wings, coiling cables.
Ask the crew kid, and you might hear: one day I'll be out there. So here's the question the scene leaves hanging. Is staying unseen a loss, something to fix as fast as you can?
Or is something happening back there that can't happen under the lights?

teach.b: Ibn Ata'illah, a Sufi teacher in Egypt, left a book of short sayings called al-Hikam, the wisdoms.
Saying eleven, paraphrased: bury your existence in the earth of obscurity, because whatever sprouts without being buried doesn't come to full flower. It's a gardener's line.

A seed left on top of the soil can sprout fast and then wilt, because nothing held it down long enough to grow roots. A buried seed looks like nothing is happening. That's exactly when the roots go down.
His word for that earth is khumul: obscurity, being unknown, off the stage for a while. Readers of the Hikam hear it as a cure for the self's hunger to be seen.
Show a good habit too early, and the applause can quietly become the reason for it. The same instinct lives in a hadith kept by al-Bukhari.

Among the people God shades on a day when there is no other shade is someone who gives in charity so quietly that the left hand doesn't know what the right hand gave. Notice what Ibn Ata'illah isn't saying.
He isn't saying never lead, never sing the solo, never be known.
He's talking about order: roots first, in the dark; flowers later, if they come at all.
So the crew kid isn't losing anything. The staircase still has to move, and something is growing back there that nobody is watching.

how: Following the hadith of the hand that gives so quietly the other hand doesn't know, Muslims try to keep some good deeds, such as charity or night prayer, private; Sufi teachers read Ibn Ata'illah's saying as training against the love of reputation.

o: staying humble by thinking little of yourself
letting good grow out of sight before it's praised
hiding your faith so nobody knows you practice

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: doesn't know what the right gave

s: Ibn Ata'illah tells people never to lead or be known
he's talking about order: roots first, out of sight; flowers later, if they come.
a hadith in al-Bukhari praises charity so quiet the left hand doesn't know what the right gave
that giver is among the people God shades on a day with no other shade.
in the saying, the seed that sprouts unburied is the one that flowers best
it's the reverse: what sprouts without being buried doesn't come to full flower.

games.q: your friends plan to hand out sandwiches at the shelter and film it for a 'giving day' post. the shelter didn't ask for a video. what fits Hikam 11?
o: film it; if it inspires one person, the post is the point.
hand out the sandwiches, skip the camera, and let it stay unseen.
don't go at all, since nobody's motives are completely pure.
games.why: the saying doesn't cancel the deed; it cancels the stage. bury it, and let the roots grow where nobody is filming.

practice: Choose one good thing you could do this week that nobody will ever trace back to you: a dish washed before anyone wakes, a kind word passed along without your name on it.
Decide exactly when you'll do it, and notice what part of you already wants to mention it later. Then let the plan sit, buried, while the breath comes and goes.

wordCard.voice: Bury yourself: Ibn Ata'illah's seed in the soil. Obscurity first, so the roots can go down before anything flowers.

orig.note: Arabic: obscurity, being unknown; the 'earth' Ibn Ata'illah tells you to bury yourself in.

carryVoice: Keep this one in your pocket: grow in the dark, where the roots don't need an audience. Three sayings of the Hikam so far.

sources.ref: Ibn Ata'illah al-Iskandari, al-Hikam, aphorism 11 (bury your existence in the earth of obscurity)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1423 (the seven whom God shades; charity so secret the left hand doesn't know)
